reasoning: This is a narrative/review article synthesizing existing literature on schizophrenia pathophysiology and treatment; it does not report generation or use of any specific research software or dataset, but rather reviews clinical and mechanistic findings from prior studies.

This is a clinical consensus guideline synthesizing existing literature and expert opinion to produce treatment recommendations. It does not generate or use any research software, nor does it create or analyze a research dataset - it reviews published evidence (systematic reviews, case reports) to form guidelines rather than conducting primary data collection or computational analysis.

The study uses an existing research software tool (TopoToolbox V2) to process a nationwide DEM, which is a utility/analysis tool rather than software created or significantly extended by the researchers, so it falls under S2. However, the research generates a new national-scale geodatabase of catchment characteristics (morphometric and topographic data) for 128 catchments across the Philippines, which is new substantive data created through the research, warranting D1 classification. Since data is generated (and used), it is classified as D1, and software is used (not generated), classified as S2.

The paper develops a new visualization tool and implements the Jaya algorithm (with Latin Hypercube Sampling enhancement) for graph drawing, a novel application generating new knowledge about algorithm performance—this constitutes generated research software (S1). It also generates synthetic datasets using the Erdős–Rényi model (varying nodes/edges) for benchmarking, in addition to using some real-world graph datasets, so new research data was created (D1) to validate the research findings.

This is a study protocol for a planned randomised clinical trial. No data has been collected yet (data collection is proposed for the future), and no research software is described as generated or used in producing results. Per the rules, protocols describing planned data/software use should be classified as S3D3 unless there is clear evidence of actual use/generation.

This is a survey/interview-based study that generated new research data through literature review, semi-structured interviews, and a survey of nurses/midwives across four cohorts (n=153) over 2019-22. This survey and interview data is newly collected/generated by the researchers, constituting substantive research data generation. There is no mention of any research software being developed or used in a substantive way to generate new knowledge (standard statistical analysis tools would be incidental utility use, not central to knowledge creation). Thus the paper fits S3 (no research software) and D1 (data generated).

The provided text is essentially just a title and journal/year information with no abstract content or further details. There is no evidence of any research software being generated or used, nor any research data being created or used, within the available text. Without any substantive description of methods, software tools, or datasets, the paper cannot be classified as generating or using software/data based on the given information.

The study uses existing software/tools (TCP modeling, treatment planning software) to analyze DW-MRI data, but generates new patient-specific research data: ADC-derived cellular density maps, TCP maps, and BTV dose escalation plans from ten GBM patients' imaging data. This novel derived data is central to producing new knowledge (increased TCP via personalized dose escalation), classifying as data generated (D1). The computational tools (TCP models, planning systems) appear to be existing/used rather than newly created research software, so S2.

This study generated new research data (multiplexed immunofluorescence profiling of immune cell phenotypes across a cohort of NLPHL and THRLBCL patient samples), producing original quantitative datasets on immune cell marker expression that constitute new knowledge about tumour microenvironment composition. The study used existing software tools (e.g., multiplex immunofluorescence imaging/analysis platforms) to generate and analyse this data, but there is no indication that new software was developed as part of the research; standard imaging/analysis software was used as a tool. Hence Software Used (S2) and Data Generated (D1).

The study collected new primary survey data from 384 startup directors/representatives using BRCS, MBI-GS, and custom Covid-19 stress questionnaires, generating a novel dataset specific to this research (D1). For analysis, they used an existing computational technique/algorithm—the GMDH neural network—to build a predictive model; while the resulting network configuration is a product of training, the GMDH methodology itself is an established algorithmic approach applied to the data rather than a newly created software tool or package, so it is classified as software used (S2) rather than generated.

The study generates new experimental data (a new X-ray crystal structure of AMG-176 bound to Mcl-1, plus NMR-based conformer analysis of the clinical inhibitors), which are substantive research data that produce new knowledge about ligand prestructuring and induced fit. While standard crystallography/NMR processing software (e.g., refinement, structure determination tools) was likely used as a utility, there is no indication that new research software was developed or that existing software itself generated novel scientific insight beyond being a standard analytical tool. Thus the paper fits No Software (S3) and Data Generated (D1).

This is a cluster RCT in which the researchers collected primary data from mothers/children via assessments at pregnancy and multiple follow-up points, generating new substantive research data (maternal/child health outcomes) to answer the research question. There is no mention of developing or significantly extending any research software; standard statistical analysis tools were presumably used only as utilities. Thus it fits No Software, Data Generated.

The study uses existing EHR datasets (UK Biobank and CPRD Gold linked to cancer registry data) to develop phenotypes (code lists/algorithms applied to existing data) and analyze symptom/test rates. While they create harmonised phenotype definitions, these are code-based classification schemes rather than newly generated research software; no new software tool is described as being built or released. The core artifact is the use of existing substantive EHR data to generate new epidemiological findings, classifying this as data used rather than generated, and no distinct research software was created.

This is a perspective/opinion piece discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum. It does not report any empirical data collection or analysis, nor does it describe the creation or use of any research software. It is a conceptual/argumentative essay with no generated or used research artefacts (software or data).

The paper presents DOCU-CLIM, a newly compiled global dataset of 621 documentary climate time series (both published and previously unpublished), representing substantive new research data that was generated through the research. While the authors used proxy forward models to evaluate the series against climate fields, the analysis is described as a method/validation approach rather than the creation or extension of research software; no new software tool is described as being developed. Thus this is a clear case of data generation without accompanying software generation.

The study generated new research data via sediment-core multilocus metabarcoding of a 100-year lake record combined with biocide/climate measurements (D1). It also developed a novel explainable multimodal neural network/AI framework (described as a conceptual framework combining network models with multimodal learning) specifically created for this research to link biodiversity dynamics with abiotic change, constituting generated research software that produced new knowledge (S1).

This is a state-of-the-art narrative review summarizing existing literature on blood-brain barrier imaging techniques and clinical applications. It does not report generation or use of any specific research software, nor does it generate or analyze a specific research dataset. It synthesizes findings from prior studies without creating new software or data artifacts.

This is a cross-sectional survey study where researchers collected original primary data from 10,007 respondents in Malang, Indonesia via a questionnaire on COVID-19 knowledge, vaccine willingness, and uptake. This constitutes newly generated research data (D1). Statistical analyses (linear regression, logistic regression, GSEM) were performed using standard statistical software, but these are utility tools not developed or substantively extended as part of the research, so no research software is generated or used in a knowledge-creating sense (S3).

This is a review article discussing concepts and challenges in post-GWAS interpretation of AD and PD risk loci. It does not report generation or use of specific research software or datasets within the paper itself; it synthesizes existing literature and discusses methodologies conceptually rather than performing new analyses or presenting new data/tools.

This is a review article summarizing existing literature on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not report generation or use of any research software, nor does it generate or analyze new research data; it synthesizes findings from prior studies.

The paper develops a novel counterfactual GAN, newly created software that generates new knowledge (synthesizing counterfactual OCT images to study retinal aging), qualifying as S1. The data used is the UK Biobank OCT imaging dataset, an existing large-scale dataset that the authors analyze retrospectively rather than generating themselves, which fits D2 (substantive data used, not newly generated).

The researchers used an existing pretrained model (GPT-2) and existing NLP metrics/tools (not creating new software, though they wrote scripts/tutorial, this is more a methodological pipeline using existing software) to generate simulated FTD-like narratives, which constitute newly generated research data (the simulated narratives and associated NLP measure outputs). Since GPT-2 and sentence embedding methods are existing research software used (not substantially extended), this is S2. The simulated narratives and analyses represent new data generated for the study, hence D1.

This is a study protocol describing a planned future survey. No actual software was developed (Qualtrics is used as a utility tool for survey distribution, not research software), and no data has yet been collected or analyzed - the survey design, dissemination, and data collection are all described as future plans. Per the criteria, planned/proposed artefacts and research protocols without evidence of actual use/generation should be classified as S3D3.

This paper reports phase 1 clinical drug-drug interaction trials in healthy subjects, generating new pharmacokinetic data (Cmax, AUC values, confidence intervals) specific to rezafungin coadministration with various drugs. This is clearly research data generated through clinical trials, producing new knowledge about drug interactions. There is no indication of any research software being created or used to generate new knowledge - standard statistical analysis tools would have been used as utilities (S3), not as research software generating new knowledge themselves. The paper is primarily a clinical/pharmacological study without software development or computational methods being central to the findings.

The study uses UK Biobank data (anthropometric, physical activity, dietary, FFQ) to derive a novel adherence score (the operationalised 2018 WCRF/AICR score) for >150,000 participants, which constitutes generation of new research data (new derived variables/scores not previously available). No new research software is created or described - standard statistical/scoring methodology is applied, so software is only used as a utility (S3). Hence D1 for generated derived data and S3 for no substantive software generation/use."

This is a literature review summarizing existing cardiovascular risk prediction methods, biomarkers, and ocular imaging approaches. It does not describe generation or use of any specific research software (no code, tools, or computational workflows created or applied), nor does it present new research data or use an existing dataset for analysis - it synthesizes findings from prior literature without producing or analyzing original data.

The study uses existing Google Trends search data (an external data source) and applies Joinpoint regression analysis (a statistical tool, not research software developed or substantively extended by the authors) to analyze it. The data used—search volume trends—was not generated by the researchers but downloaded from an existing public platform, constituting used data that generates new knowledge about health information seeking behavior. No new research software was created; the analysis tool (Joinpoint) is used as a standard statistical utility rather than being developed or extended as part of the research.

This qualitative study collected new interview data from 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers via semi-structured interviews, generating original research data (interview transcripts/themes) specific to this study - fitting D1. The analysis was done via "manual thematic analysis," with no mention of specialized research software being created or used for analysis beyond standard tools, so it falls under S3 (no research software).

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes data extracted from 76 articles and 2 national surveys to compute pooled prevalence estimates (stunting, thinness, overweight/obesity, micronutrient deficiencies). The meta-analysis process generates new aggregated data (pooled prevalence statistics, new knowledge about nutrition patterns) from existing literature, which counts as substantive data generation (D1). No research software was developed or used in a substantive way to create new knowledge beyond standard statistical tools for meta-analysis, so it falls under S3 (no distinct research software generated/used for knowledge creation beyond routine statistical packages).

The study generated new experimental data (motor unit firing characteristics from high-density sEMG recordings in TD and DCD children) specifically collected for this research, constituting newly generated research data (D1). The researchers used existing decomposition software/algorithms (e.g., EMG decomposition tools) to process signals, but there's no indication they developed new research software themselves - they used established analysis tools/software to generate new knowledge from their experiments (S2). Thus the paper fits Software Used, Data Generated.
